lab_title: The Double Helix and Semiconservative Replication of DNA
top_level_objectives: Describe the three-dimensional structure of the DNA double helix, including the antiparallel sugar-phosphate backbones and inward-projecting nitrogenous bases
Apply the complementary base-pairing rules (A-T via two hydrogen bonds, G-C via three) and explain how they enforce strand complementarity
Explain how the directionality of the sugar-phosphate backbone (5' to 3' versus 3' to 5') produces the antiparallel arrangement of the two strands
Trace the roles of helicase, single-strand binding proteins, DNA polymerase, and DNA ligase at the replication fork
Explain why the antiparallel structure forces continuous leading-strand and discontinuous lagging-strand (Okazaki fragment) synthesis
Define semiconservative replication and justify why each daughter molecule contains one parental and one new strand

scenes.brief_purpose: Orient students to the overall three-dimensional form of DNA and establish the vocabulary of its major structural features before dissecting them.
key_visuals: A large, slowly rotating B-form double helix floating at eye level
Two colored sugar-phosphate backbones spiraling around a shared central axis
Rungs of paired bases visible between the backbones
A translucent axis line running through the center of the helix
student_actions: Rotate and orbit the floating helix to view it from multiple angles
Tap the two backbones and the base-pair rungs to reveal introductory labels
Identify which parts are the backbone and which are the bases

scenes.scene_name: Inside the Backbone: Sugar, Phosphate, and Directionality
scenes.brief_purpose: Zoom into the backbone to show that it is built from alternating sugars and phosphates and that this chain has an inherent 5'-to-3' direction.
key_visuals: A magnified single strand showing alternating deoxyribose sugars and phosphate groups
Numbered carbons on a highlighted sugar with the 5' and 3' positions emphasized
Directional arrows pointing along the strand from the 5' end to the 3' end
The complementary strand faded in the background running the opposite direction
student_actions: Trace the alternating sugar-phosphate pattern along the strand
Tag the 5' end and 3' end of the highlighted strand
Observe how the two strands' arrows point in opposite directions to introduce the idea of antiparallel orientation

scenes.scene_name: Base Pairing and the Antiparallel Rule
scenes.brief_purpose: Let students discover the complementary base-pairing rules and connect base pairing to the antiparallel arrangement of the two strands.
key_visuals: Four color-coded bases (A, T, G, C) available as draggable pieces
An A-T pair snapping together with two hydrogen bonds and a G-C pair with three hydrogen bonds
A short open helix segment with unpaired bases waiting to be matched
Directional 5'-to-3' arrows shown on both strands to reinforce the antiparallel layout
student_actions: Drag bases into place to correctly pair A with T and G with C across the helix
Count and confirm the number of hydrogen bonds in each pair
Verify that a completed segment has one strand running 5' to 3' and its partner running 3' to 5'

scenes.brief_purpose: Begin replication by showing how the double helix is opened and the exposed single strands are stabilized.
key_visuals: Helicase moving along the helix and separating the two strands into a Y-shaped replication fork
Single-strand binding proteins coating the exposed template strands
A widening bubble of unwound DNA with labeled parental strands
Highlighted 5' and 3' orientations of each exposed template strand
student_actions: Activate helicase and watch the fork open
Place single-strand binding proteins onto the exposed strands
Note the opposite orientations of the two template strands in preparation for synthesis

scenes.brief_purpose: Demonstrate how DNA polymerase's 5'-to-3'-only synthesis, combined with antiparallel templates, forces different synthesis modes on the two strands.
key_visuals: DNA polymerase adding nucleotides continuously along the leading-strand template toward the fork
Lagging-strand polymerase working in short backward bursts producing Okazaki fragments
DNA ligase sealing the gaps between adjacent Okazaki fragments
Directional arrows contrasting continuous versus discontinuous synthesis
student_actions: Guide polymerase along the leading strand and observe continuous synthesis
Assemble Okazaki fragments on the lagging strand in the correct 5'-to-3' direction
Use DNA ligase to join fragments and explain why the two strands are built differently

scenes.brief_purpose: Synthesize the lab's core concept by showing that each daughter molecule contains one parental and one newly-made strand, and assess understanding.
key_visuals: Two completed daughter double helices side by side
Parental strands shown in the original color and new strands in a distinct color within each daughter
A summary diagram tracing one old and one new strand into each product
A short quiz panel with base-pairing and strand-orientation questions
student_actions: Color-code or tag the parental versus newly synthesized strand in each daughter molecule
Explain in a prompt why the process is called semiconservative
Answer summary questions linking antiparallel structure to leading/lagging synthesis
